notes: HOW LHS VALUES WORK (SISEPUEDE mechanics): Each L feature value is the MAGNITUDE of a transformation TARGET to be achieved by the END of the simulation (2070). The variable does NOT jump instantly — SISEPUEDE uses a vec_implementation_ramp (linear or sigmoid) to transition the variable progressively from its baseline value toward the 2070 target over n_tp_ramp time periods (typically 20–30 years). The emission outputs at 2033–2037 and 2066–2070 are the ACTUAL ANNUAL EMISSIONS at those moments in the simulation — they reflect the ramp in progress.

L feature scale: 0.0 = target is baseline (no change), 1.0 = target is maximum possible transformation by 2070. E.g. L=0.9 for renewable electricity means the model ramps Uganda to 90% of maximum renewable ambition by 2070, with gradual change from baseline along the way.

X features (exogenous) scale: -1.0 = fixed baseline trajectory (no uncertainty), 0.0–1.0 = LHS uncertainty draw (low to high outcome). These represent different plausible future states, not policy levers.
Each group covers multiple underlying SISEPUEDE variables that move together — they cannot be set independently. This is a known limitation of the grouped trajectory approach.

Emission outputs (2033–2037 avg, 2066–2070 avg) are actual annual emissions AT those points in the simulation. Near-term (2033–37) reflects partially-implemented policies mid-ramp. Long-term (2066–70) reflects near-fully implemented policies close to the 2070 target.
There is a 30-year gap (2038–2065) with no emission predictions. Mid-century (e.g. 2050) cannot be directly estimated.
Design IDs (0–4) were used to generate training data with different L/X transformation rules. The model does not use design_id as a feature — any combination in the valid ranges is acceptable.
BAU baseline uses L=0.1 (minimal policy ambition target for 2070) and X=-1.0 (fixed baseline futures).
Truncated group names (3, 8, 9, 57) reflect incomplete SISEPUEDE variable labels in the source data — their policies are identified from transformation codes.

l_transform.reverse: x = (T - b) / m  (then clamp x to [0,1])

1.training_column: group_1_L_:math:\text{CH}_4 Crop Anaerobic Decomposition Emission Factor
1.semantic_min: Baseline CH₄ emissions from flooded rice paddies — no water management interventions.
1.semantic_max: Maximum reduction of methane from rice cultivation through alternate wetting/drying, crop variety changes.
1.policy_description: Controls how aggressively Uganda reduces methane from rice paddy cultivation. At 1.0, the rice sector achieves its maximum technically feasible methane abatement by the end of the simulation period.
1.transformer_default_magnitude_descriptio: Minimum fraction of rice under improved management (CH4 reduction)
1.physical_at_L1: 0.45 — Minimum fraction of rice under improved management (CH4 reduction)
1.physical_at_L0: 0.045 — Minimum fraction of rice under improved management (CH4 reduction)

2.training_column: group_2_L_Fraction of Food Produced Lost Before Consumption
2.semantic_min: Baseline post-harvest losses (estimated ~30% of production lost before consumption).
2.semantic_max: Maximum reduction in food loss across the entire supply chain — storage, transport, processing.
2.policy_description: Reducing food loss cuts the agricultural emissions needed to produce a given amount of food. At 1.0, Uganda achieves its maximum feasible reduction in pre-consumption food loss.

3.semantic_min: Conventional tillage with full crop residue burning.
3.semantic_max: Maximum adoption of no-till practices and elimination of crop residue burning.
3.policy_description: Conservation agriculture reduces soil disturbance and eliminates burning. At 1.0, Uganda achieves maximum no-till coverage and zero residue burning. Note: training column name is truncated in source data.
3.transformer_default_magnitude_descriptio: No-till adoption by crop + final burned/removed residue fractions
3.physical_at_L1: full default (magnitude_burned=0.0, magnitude_removed=0.5) — No-till adoption by crop + final burned/removed residue fractions
3.physical_at_L0: scales toward baseline (default=magnitude_burned=0.0, magnitude_removed=0.5) — No-till adoption by crop + final burned/removed residue fractions

4.semantic_min: Baseline crop yields — no productivity improvements beyond trend.
4.semantic_max: Maximum achievable yield improvement through better seeds, inputs, and practices.
4.policy_description: Higher yields mean less land needed to produce the same food, reducing land-use emissions. At 1.0, Uganda achieves its maximum technically feasible yield improvement.

5.training_column: group_5_L_Annual Capture and Sequestration by Type
5.semantic_min: No CCS deployed — baseline with no engineered carbon removal.
5.semantic_max: Maximum CCS capacity deployed — full build-out of carbon capture infrastructure.
5.policy_description: Direct carbon capture from air or point sources. In Uganda's context this is primarily biological/forestry-based sequestration potential. At 1.0, maximum feasible capture capacity is deployed.
5.transformer_default_magnitude_descriptio: Total DAC capacity at full implementation (megatonnes)
5.physical_at_L1: 50 Mt — Total DAC capacity at full implementation (megatonnes)
5.physical_at_L0: 5 Mt — Total DAC capacity at full implementation (megatonnes)
5.transformer_magnitude_note: Unit is megatonnes of CO2 (DAC capacity), not a dimensionless fraction.

6.semantic_min: Baseline grid transmission losses (Uganda currently has losses ~20-30%).
6.semantic_max: Minimum achievable transmission losses through grid modernisation and smart grid investment.
6.policy_description: Reducing losses means less generation is needed for the same delivered energy. At 1.0, Uganda achieves its technically feasible minimum grid loss rate.
6.transformer_default_magnitude_descriptio: Transmission loss level (final value by default)
6.physical_at_L1: 0.06 (6% grid loss target; lower = better) — Transmission loss level (final value by default)
6.physical_at_L0: 0.006 (0.6% grid loss target; lower = better) — Transmission loss level (final value by default)
6.transformer_magnitude_note: Lower transmission loss target = better grid efficiency. L=1.0 targets 6% losses; L=0.1 (BAU) targets 0.6% losses.

7.semantic_min: No clean hydrogen in the energy mix.
7.semantic_max: Maximum clean hydrogen production target for energy supply.
7.policy_description: Controls the minimum share of clean hydrogen in energy production. At 1.0, Uganda deploys its maximum planned clean hydrogen capacity. This is a NemoMod model parameter (energy system model).

7.physical_at_L1: 0.95 — Target share of clean hydrogen (default electrolysis)
7.physical_at_L0: 0.095 — Target share of clean hydrogen (default electrolysis)

8.semantic_min: Baseline renewable electricity share (Uganda ~85% hydro-based today).
8.semantic_max: Maximum renewable electricity target — full deployment of solar, wind, geothermal alongside hydro.
8.policy_description: Controls the minimum share and production targets for renewable electricity. Uganda already has significant hydro but this lever covers expansion to other renewables. Note: column name truncated in source data.
8.transformer_default_magnitude_descriptio: Minimum renewable share of electricity at full implementation
8.physical_at_L1: 0.95 — Minimum renewable share of electricity at full implementation
8.physical_at_L0: 0.095 — Minimum renewable share of electricity at full implementation

9.semantic_min: Baseline fugitive methane leaks from fossil fuel extraction and distribution.
9.semantic_max: Maximum reduction of fugitive leaks through detection, repair, and infrastructure upgrades.
9.policy_description: Fugitive methane is a potent near-term climate forcer. At 1.0, Uganda achieves maximum feasible leak reduction. Note: column name truncated in source data.

10.semantic_max: Maximum fraction of non-fugitive CH₄ flared rather than vented (flaring converts CH₄ to CO₂, lower GWP).
10.policy_description: Flaring methane instead of venting it reduces its climate impact ~25x (CH₄ GWP vs CO₂). At 1.0, all venting that can be flared is flared.

11.semantic_min: Baseline forest sequestration — current forest management practices.
11.semantic_max: Maximum enhanced sequestration through improved forest management, species selection, density.

11.physical_at_L0: 0.005 — Fractional increase in forest sequestration factors

19.physical_at_L0: 0.099999 — Target self-transition probability for primary forest

53.policy_description: Reducing food thrown away by consumers decreases the organic material going to landfills and open dumps. At 1.0, maximum feasible per-capita food waste reduction is achieved.

62.semantic_min_neg1: Fixed baseline GDP trajectory (the SSP-aligned baseline — no uncertainty).
62.semantic_0: Low GDP growth scenario (pessimistic economic development).
62.semantic_1: High GDP growth scenario (optimistic economic development).
62.policy_description: Represents the range of possible GDP trajectories for Uganda between 2025 and 2070. Higher GDP drives more energy demand, industrial activity, and transport — but also more resources for clean investment. IMPORTANT: This is a relative scale, not an absolute GDP figure. 1.0 does not mean 100% GDP increase — it represents the highest GDP scenario in the LHS uncertainty range.
62.scalar_range_note: Pending — scalar bounds not available from S3 or modeler. Must confirm with Tony.
62.agent_narrative_X0: Low economic growth scenario: Uganda GDP grows more slowly than the $679B central 2050 projection, moderating energy demand, urbanisation pressure, and industrial emissions.
62.agent_narrative_X1: High economic growth scenario: Uganda GDP exceeds the $679B central 2050 projection, accelerating energy demand, industrial activity, and emissions pressure — but also expanding fiscal capacity for climate investment.

63.semantic_0: Low elasticity — industrial production grows less than GDP.
63.semantic_1: High elasticity — industrial production grows faster than GDP.
63.policy_description: Controls how strongly industrial production (cement, chemicals, metals, paper, etc.) responds to GDP growth. High values mean more industrialisation per unit of GDP, driving more process emissions. This is an exogenous uncertainty about Uganda's industrial development pathway.

64.semantic_0: Low product use growth per GDP — more service-based economy.
64.semantic_1: High product use per GDP — more material-intensive consumption growth.
64.policy_description: Controls how strongly product use (lubricants, refrigerants, paraffin wax, etc.) grows with per-capita GDP. Higher values imply more consumption of industrial products as incomes rise.

65.semantic_1: High population growth scenario (Uganda high ~90M+ by 2050).
65.policy_description: Represents Uganda's uncertain population trajectory (rural and urban). Population is a key driver of food demand, waste generation, energy use, and transport. Uganda is one of the world's fastest-growing populations. IMPORTANT: Like GDP, this is a relative scale in the LHS uncertainty range, not absolute population figures.

65.agent_narrative_X0: Low population scenario: Uganda's population grows more slowly than the 85.8M central 2050 projection, moderating demand for food, energy, water, and transport infrastructure.
65.agent_narrative_X1: High population scenario: Uganda's population exceeds the 85.8M central 2050 projection, amplifying pressure on energy systems, food security, urban infrastructure, and emissions from land use.

66.semantic_min_neg1: Fixed baseline building energy demand trajectory.
66.semantic_0: Low building energy demand growth per income — decoupling of energy and wealth.
66.semantic_1: High building energy demand growth with income — rapid appliance uptake and electrification.
66.policy_description: Controls how strongly residential and commercial energy demand (appliances and heat) grows with GDP per capita. High values mean rapidly increasing building energy use as incomes rise (more refrigerators, ACs, etc.).

67.semantic_0: Low freight growth with GDP — efficient logistics, shorter supply chains.
67.semantic_1: High freight growth with GDP — rapid increase in goods movement as economy expands.
67.policy_description: Controls the elasticity of freight transport demand (tonne-km) to GDP growth. High values mean more freight movement as Uganda's economy grows.

68.semantic_0: Low travel demand growth per income — compact cities, low private vehicle adoption.
68.semantic_1: High passenger travel growth — rapid motorization and long-distance travel growth as incomes rise.
68.policy_description: Controls how much passenger travel demand (person-km) grows with GDP per capita. High values imply rapid growth in private vehicle ownership and long-distance travel as Uganda's population becomes wealthier.

emission_total_sum.description: Sum of all annual GHG emissions across all sectors for the full model period 2015–2070 (56 years). IMPORTANT: The 2015–2024 historical period (10 years) is included and is IDENTICAL across all scenarios — it adds a fixed offset. Only 2025–2070 responds to policy choices. Use this metric for comparisons between scenarios, not as a standalone absolute figure. The policy-relevant mitigation is best read from the % change vs baseline.
emission_total_sum.policy_context: Lower values mean Uganda contributes less to global warming. Because all scenarios share the same 2015–2024 history, scenario differences fully reflect policy impact over 2025–2070. The gap between BAU and Net Zero represents Uganda's total mitigation potential.

2033_2037_mean_emission.description: Average of ACTUAL ANNUAL emissions across 2033, 2034, 2035, 2036, 2037. These are real emission values at those moments in the simulation — NOT targets. At this point, SISEPUEDE policies are partway through their implementation ramp toward the 2070 target (perhaps 30–60% implemented depending on the ramp shape). Emissions reflect where Uganda is mid-transition.
2033_2037_mean_emission.policy_context: Most relevant to Uganda's NDC targets (~2030 period). Shows what emissions look like when policies are partially implemented — a critical check on near-term ambition.

2066_2070_mean_emission.description: Average of ACTUAL ANNUAL emissions across 2066, 2067, 2068, 2069, 2070. These are real emission values near the END of the simulation — the moment when policies are close to fully implemented (near their 2070 targets). This is the best indicator of what Uganda's emissions look like once all policies reach their intended scale. NOTE: There is a 30-year gap (2038–2065) with no emission data — mid-century (2050) cannot be directly read.
2066_2070_mean_emission.policy_context: Represents Uganda's long-term emission pathway at near-full policy implementation. Wide range (62–206 Mt/yr) shows transformative impact of ambitious vs. weak policies.

2025_2035_mean_benefits.description: Average annual monetary value of non-climate co-benefits from 2025–2035: air quality improvements, health benefits, reduced congestion, and avoided health costs.
2025_2035_mean_benefits.policy_context: Co-benefits often exceed mitigation costs. A near-term focus on co-benefits (especially air pollution and health) can build political support for climate action.

2025_2070_mean_benefits.description: Average annual monetary value of co-benefits across the full 2025–2070 period.
2025_2070_mean_benefits.policy_context: Over the full period, co-benefits range from 16–25 billion USD/year, dwarfing implementation costs. This is a powerful argument for ambitious climate policy.

2025_2035_mean_costs.description: Average annual cost of implementing climate policies from 2025–2035, including both technical and system costs.
2025_2035_mean_costs.policy_context: Near-term costs are modest (0.39–0.52 billion USD/year) relative to co-benefits (2.77–3.34 billion USD/year), suggesting a strong economic case for early action.

2025_2070_mean_costs.description: Average annual cost of implementing climate policies over the full 2025–2070 period.
2025_2070_mean_costs.policy_context: Long-term costs vary significantly (0.56–1.62 billion/year) depending on ambition level. Even at maximum, costs represent a small fraction of projected GDP.

2025_2035_max_costs_rel_to_gdp.display_name: Peak Near-Term Cost as % of GDP (2025–2035)
2025_2035_max_costs_rel_to_gdp.description: Maximum single-year implementation cost as a fraction of GDP in the 2025–2035 period. Model outputs this as a decimal fraction (e.g. 0.003 = 0.3%). The UI multiplies by 100 for display.
2025_2035_max_costs_rel_to_gdp.policy_context: Even at maximum ambition, peak costs are under 0.54% of GDP in the near term — comparable to international climate finance commitments.

2025_2070_max_costs_rel_to_gdp.display_name: Peak Long-Term Cost as % of GDP (2025–2070)
2025_2070_max_costs_rel_to_gdp.description: Maximum single-year implementation cost as a fraction of GDP across the full 2025–2070 period. Model outputs as decimal fraction.
2025_2070_max_costs_rel_to_gdp.policy_context: Long-term peak cost reaches at most 0.71% of GDP — well within the range of what Uganda could finance with domestic revenues plus international climate finance.

2025_2035_cumulative_cost_rel_to_gdp.display_name: Cumulative Near-Term Cost as % of GDP (2025–2035)
2025_2035_cumulative_cost_rel_to_gdp.description: Total cumulative implementation costs from 2025–2035 expressed as fraction of annual GDP. Model outputs as decimal fraction.
2025_2035_cumulative_cost_rel_to_gdp.policy_context: Cumulative costs of 0.20–0.31% of GDP over 10 years represent a manageable public investment, particularly given access to international climate finance.

2025_2070_cumulative_cost_rel_to_gdp.display_name: Cumulative Long-Term Cost as % of GDP (2025–2070)
2025_2070_cumulative_cost_rel_to_gdp.description: Total cumulative implementation costs from 2025–2070 expressed as fraction of annual GDP. Model outputs as decimal fraction.
2025_2070_cumulative_cost_rel_to_gdp.policy_context: Over the full 45-year period, cumulative costs decline as a GDP fraction because Uganda's economy grows faster than costs. This confirms the long-term affordability of ambitious climate action.

bau.name: Business as Usual (BAU)
bau.description: Minimal policy action with baseline future trajectories. Represents Uganda's emissions path if current limited policies continue.

moderate.name: Moderate Ambition
moderate.description: Moderate policy action across all sectors with median uncertainty futures. A middle-of-the-road scenario.

netzero.name: Near Net Zero
netzero.description: Per-group L values derived from Uganda's NZ strategy YAML files. Groups not activated in the NZ pathway remain at BAU (0.1). X features use median futures (0.5).
